def: A list of topics to discuss at a meeting.
ex: Please send me the agenda before the meeting so I can prepare my questions.
nat: The first item on the agenda is next quarter's budget.

mis.bad: I have a busy agenda today at the office.
mis.good: I have a busy schedule today at the office.
mis.why: An agenda is a list of meeting topics, not a personal daily schedule.

def: A person who goes to an event or meeting.
ex: All the attendees received a copy of the slides after the presentation ended.
nat: Each attendee must sign in at the front desk.

mis.bad: The assistants of the meeting were very quiet.
mis.good: The attendees of the meeting were very quiet.
mis.why: Assistant means a helper; people who attend a meeting are attendees.

def: To formally end a meeting or stop it until a later time.
ex: The chairman adjourned the meeting at noon and we all went to lunch.
nat: Let's adjourn until tomorrow morning and continue then.

mis.bad: We adjourned the project because we had no budget.
mis.good: We suspended the project because we had no budget.
mis.why: Adjourn is mostly used for meetings and courts, not for stopping a project.

def: To change the time or date of a planned event.
ex: I had to reschedule our call because my flight was delayed by two hours.
nat: Could we reschedule for Thursday afternoon instead?

mis.bad: Can we reschedule the meeting to the next week?
mis.good: Can we reschedule the meeting for next week?
mis.why: Use "reschedule for" with a new time; "to the next week" sounds unnatural.

def: A short summary of the main points of something.
ex: Before we continue, here is a quick recap of what we decided yesterday.
nat: Could someone give me a recap of the meeting?

mis.bad: Let me do a resume of yesterday's discussion.
mis.good: Let me do a recap of yesterday's discussion.
mis.why: "Resume" is a false friend in this sense; a short summary is a recap.

def: To make a process easier, or to lead a group discussion.
ex: Maria facilitated the workshop and made sure everyone had a chance to speak.
nat: Good software can facilitate communication between departments.

mis.bad: The new tool facilitates to share files.
mis.good: The new tool makes it easier to share files.
mis.why: Facilitate takes a direct object and is not followed by "to + verb".

def: The official written record of what was said in a meeting.
ex: Sam took the minutes during the call and emailed them to everyone afterward.
nat: The minutes show that we agreed to postpone the launch.

mis.bad: I will write the ata of the meeting.
mis.good: I will write the minutes of the meeting.
mis.why: The record of a meeting is called the minutes, always plural.

def: A person who leads a discussion and makes sure rules are followed.
ex: The moderator asked each speaker to keep their answer under two minutes.
nat: She works as a moderator for an online forum.

mis.bad: The moderator of the company is Mr. Silva.
mis.good: The head of the company is Mr. Silva.
mis.why: A moderator guides a discussion; it does not mean a company leader.

def: A new offer made after rejecting an earlier offer.
ex: The company made a counteroffer of five percent more than the first salary.
nat: He was tempted to accept the counteroffer and stay.

mis.bad: They did a counter proposal and I accepted.
mis.good: They made a counteroffer and I accepted.
mis.why: Use the verb "make" with counteroffer, and spell it as one noun.

def: Something you agree to give up to reach an agreement.
ex: Both sides had to make concessions before they could sign the contract.
nat: The union refused to make any concession on pay.

mis.bad: They did some concessions to close the deal.
mis.good: They made some concessions to close the deal.
mis.why: The usual verb is "make" a concession, not "do".

def: To admit that something is true, or to give up something.
ex: After a long argument, the manager finally conceded that our plan was better.
nat: I'll concede the point, but I still disagree with you.

mis.bad: I conceded to him that he was right.
mis.good: I conceded that he was right.
mis.why: With a "that" clause, concede does not need "to him"; avoid extra prepositions.

def: A situation where no agreement can be reached.
ex: The talks ended in deadlock because neither side would lower its price.
nat: A third party was called in to break the deadlock.

mis.bad: The negotiation arrived in a deadlock.
mis.good: The negotiation ended in deadlock.
mis.why: Use "in deadlock", not "arrive in a deadlock".

def: A situation in which neither side can win or make progress.
ex: The two teams reached a stalemate and nobody knew how to move forward.
nat: We need fresh ideas to end this stalemate.

mis.bad: The talks are in a stale mate.
mis.good: The talks are in a stalemate.
mis.why: It is one word, stalemate, not "stale mate".

def: To argue about the price of something to get a lower one.
ex: We haggled for twenty minutes before the supplier agreed to a ten percent discount.
nat: It is common to haggle at open markets.

mis.bad: He haggled the price with the seller.
mis.good: He haggled with the seller over the price.
mis.why: Haggle is intransitive: use "haggle with someone over something".

def: An offer to do work or buy something for a stated price.
ex: Our firm submitted a bid for the new airport contract last week.
nat: Their bid was too high, so they lost the project.

mis.bad: We made a bid to the government contract.
mis.good: We made a bid for the government contract.
mis.why: The noun bid is followed by "for" a contract, not "to".

def: To help two sides reach an agreement.
ex: A neutral lawyer mediated between the company and the angry supplier.
nat: HR tried to mediate the dispute between the two managers.

mis.bad: The manager mediated the two employees.
mis.good: The manager mediated between the two employees.
mis.why: Mediate needs "between" when naming both sides.

def: A final demand with a threat of what will happen if it is refused.
ex: The client gave us an ultimatum: fix the bug by Friday or cancel the contract.
nat: He issued an ultimatum to his team.

mis.bad: The client put us an ultimatum.
mis.good: The client gave us an ultimatum.
mis.why: Use "give" or "issue" an ultimatum, not "put".

def: A separate part of a legal document or contract.
ex: There is a clause in the contract that allows either side to cancel.
nat: Read the termination clause carefully before you sign.

mis.bad: I read the clausule of the agreement twice.
mis.good: I read the clause of the agreement twice.
mis.why: The English word is clause; "clausule" does not exist.

def: The conditions of an agreement, such as price and duration.
ex: Both companies agreed on the terms of the deal after three weeks of talks.
nat: Please read the terms and conditions before you accept.

mis.bad: The terms of payment is thirty days.
mis.good: The terms of payment are thirty days.
mis.why: Terms is plural in this meaning, so it takes a plural verb.

def: A process where a neutral person decides a dispute.
ex: The two companies agreed to settle the dispute through arbitration instead of court.
nat: The case went to arbitration last spring.

mis.bad: The firms went to the arbitrage to solve the issue.
mis.good: The firms went to arbitration to solve the issue.
mis.why: Arbitrage is a financial term; the legal process is arbitration.

def: An official agreement that ends a dispute.
ex: The two companies reached a settlement and avoided a long and costly trial.
nat: They agreed to a financial settlement.

mis.bad: We settled the dispute with a good settlement.
mis.good: We reached a good settlement in the dispute.
mis.why: Use "reach a settlement" as a natural collocation.

def: A person who formally asks for a job or a place.
ex: More than two hundred applicants sent their résumés for the designer position.
nat: Each applicant must complete an online form.

mis.bad: The applicant of the job was very nervous.
mis.good: The applicant for the job was very nervous.
mis.why: Use "applicant for" a job, not "of".

def: A person being considered for a job or election.
ex: The strongest candidate had ten years of experience in customer support.
nat: We interviewed five candidates this week.

mis.bad: I was candidate to the job.
mis.good: I was a candidate for the job.
mis.why: Use "a candidate for" and do not forget the article.

def: To find and persuade people to join a company.
ex: The firm recruited twenty engineers from universities in the last six months.
nat: We are trying to recruit a new sales manager.

mis.bad: They recruited me to be their new supervisor.
mis.good: They recruited me as their new supervisor.
mis.why: Use "recruit someone as" a role, not "to be" in this typical context.

def: A person whose job is to find new employees.
ex: A recruiter called me yesterday about an interesting position in Lisbon.
nat: The recruiter asked about my salary expectations.

mis.bad: I talked to the recrutador this morning.
mis.good: I talked to the recruiter this morning.
mis.why: The English word is recruiter, not a copy of the Portuguese noun.

def: The person who asks the questions in a job interview.
ex: The interviewer asked me why I wanted to leave my previous company.
nat: Look at the interviewer when you answer.

mis.bad: The interviewer made a question about my experience.
mis.good: The interviewer asked a question about my experience.
mis.why: Questions are asked, not made, in English.

def: A trial period at the start of a new job.
ex: New employees must pass a three-month probation period before getting a permanent contract.
nat: She is still on probation at her new company.

mis.bad: I am in experience period at my new job.
mis.good: I am on probation at my new job.
mis.why: In English you are "on probation", not in an "experience period".

def: Money paid to an employee who loses their job.
ex: He received six months of severance pay when the company closed his department.
nat: They negotiated a generous severance package.

mis.bad: He received an indemnity when he was fired.
mis.good: He received severance pay when he was fired.
mis.why: Severance pay is the normal term for money paid after a dismissal.

def: A moment when a company ends jobs because there is not enough work.
ex: The company announced layoffs affecting nearly ten percent of its staff.
nat: After the layoff, morale was very low.

mis.bad: Many people did a layoff last month.
mis.good: Many people were laid off last month.
mis.why: Lay off is a verb phrase used in the passive; people do not "do" a layoff.

def: Without a job because the work is no longer needed (UK).
ex: Thirty workers were made redundant after the factory moved overseas last year.
nat: Her position became redundant after the merger.

mis.bad: I was fired because my position was redundancy.
mis.good: I was made redundant because my position was no longer needed.
mis.why: Redundant is the adjective; redundancy is the noun, and being made redundant is not being fired for fault.

def: A long break from work, often to study or travel.
ex: After ten years at the university, she took a sabbatical to write a book.
nat: He is on sabbatical until next September.

mis.bad: I will take a sabbath year to travel.
mis.good: I will take a sabbatical year to travel.
mis.why: The word for a long career break is sabbatical, not sabbath.

def: Working for different clients instead of one employer.
ex: She works as a freelance translator and chooses her own projects and hours.
nat: He went freelance after leaving the agency.

mis.bad: I work like freelancer in design.
mis.good: I work as a freelancer in design.
mis.why: Use "as" for a role or job; "like" means "similar to".

def: A person you work with.
ex: My colleagues organized a surprise party for me when I finished the project.
nat: She is a former colleague of mine.

mis.bad: I have a good relation with my collegues.
mis.good: I have a good relationship with my colleagues.
mis.why: Relation and relationship differ; also colleague has a different spelling in English.

pt: força de trabalho, quadro de funcionários
def: All the people who work for a company or in a country.
ex: The company's workforce grew from fifty to three hundred in just two years.
nat: A skilled workforce is essential to our growth.

mis.bad: The workforce of our company are very young.
mis.good: The workforce of our company is very young.
mis.why: Workforce is treated as a singular noun here.

def: A list of employees and the money paid to them.
ex: The payroll department sends everyone their payslip on the fifth of each month.
nat: We have forty people on the payroll.

mis.bad: We have fifty people in the payroll.
mis.good: We have fifty people on the payroll.
mis.why: The preposition is "on" the payroll.

def: Money paid regularly to a worker, usually by the hour or week.
ex: The minimum wage in this country has risen twice in the past three years.
nat: Many workers want a higher wage.

mis.bad: My wage is five thousand reais per year.
mis.good: My salary is sixty thousand reais per year.
mis.why: Wage is usually hourly or weekly; a yearly fixed amount is a salary.

def: Extra hours worked beyond normal working time.
ex: We worked a lot of overtime last month to finish the delivery on schedule.
nat: Is overtime paid in your company?

mis.bad: I made many extra hours this week.
mis.good: I worked a lot of overtime this week.
mis.why: English uses "work overtime", not "make extra hours".

def: A fixed period of time during which a group of workers is on duty.
ex: My shift starts at six in the morning and finishes at two.
nat: Nurses often work the night shift.

mis.bad: I work in the turn of the night.
mis.good: I work the night shift.
mis.why: Work turns in Portuguese are shifts in English.

def: Extra money given to an employee as a reward.
ex: Everyone on the team received a bonus after we reached our annual targets.
nat: She gets a yearly bonus.

mis.bad: I received a bonification this month.
mis.good: I received a bonus this month.
mis.why: The English word for the extra reward is bonus.

def: An extra benefit you get because of your job.
ex: Free lunch and flexible hours are some of the perks of working here.
nat: One perk of the job is the gym membership.

mis.bad: The company offers many benefices like gym.
mis.good: The company offers many perks like a gym.
mis.why: Everyday English for job extras is perks or benefits, not "benefices".

def: An official evaluation of how well an employee works.
ex: My annual appraisal is next week, and my manager will discuss my goals.
nat: The appraisal showed that she was ready for promotion.

mis.bad: I had the evaluation of the performance with my boss.
mis.good: I had a performance appraisal with my boss.
mis.why: The usual collocation is performance appraisal or review.

def: To give someone a higher position, or to advertise a product.
ex: She was promoted to senior engineer after only two years at the company.
nat: They promote their products on social media.

mis.bad: He was promoted for manager last year.
mis.good: He was promoted to manager last year.
mis.why: The preposition after promote is "to" a new role.

def: To move someone to a lower position as a punishment.
ex: He was demoted to assistant after he lost an important client.
nat: Nobody wants to be demoted.

mis.bad: He was demoted for assistant.
mis.good: He was demoted to assistant.
mis.why: After demote, use "to" the lower rank.

def: The act of formally leaving your job.
ex: She handed in her resignation on Monday and left at the end of the month.
nat: His resignation surprised everyone in the office.

mis.bad: I presented my demission to the director.
mis.good: I handed in my resignation to the director.
mis.why: Use "hand in" or "submit" a resignation; "demission" is not used.

def: The time someone holds a job or position.
ex: During his tenure as director, the company doubled its sales.
nat: She has a long tenure at this firm.

mis.bad: During his tenure of manager, we grew a lot.
mis.good: During his tenure as manager, we grew a lot.
mis.why: Use "as" before a role after tenure.

def: Higher rank or longer service in a company.
ex: Promotions in this office depend more on seniority than on performance.
nat: Her seniority gave her the best desk.

mis.bad: He has big seniority in the company.
mis.good: He has a lot of seniority in the company.
mis.why: Seniority is uncountable and takes "a lot of", not "big".

def: A person who is learning a job by doing it.
ex: The company hired three trainees who will rotate between departments for a year.
nat: He started as a management trainee.

mis.bad: He is a trainer in our firm, learning the work.
mis.good: He is a trainee in our firm, learning the work.
mis.why: Trainer teaches; the person learning is the trainee.

def: A person who learns a skill by working for a skilled person.
ex: He began as an apprentice electrician and became a qualified professional in four years.
nat: The apprentice watched the master carefully.

mis.bad: He is apprentice of the carpenter.
mis.good: He is an apprentice to the carpenter.
mis.why: Use an article and "apprentice to" a person.

def: Meeting people to make useful professional contacts.
ex: Networking at conferences helped me find my first client in the industry.
nat: Good networking can open many doors.

mis.bad: I did a lot of network in the event.
mis.good: I did a lot of networking at the event.
mis.why: The activity is networking; "network" is the noun for the group.

def: Special skill or knowledge in a particular subject.
ex: Her expertise in data security made her the ideal person to lead the audit.
nat: We need someone with legal expertise.

mis.bad: He has a big expertise in marketing.
mis.good: He has a lot of expertise in marketing.
mis.why: Expertise is uncountable, so use "a lot of", not "a big".

def: Able to do something well because of training and practice.
ex: To apply, you must be proficient in Excel and fluent in English.
nat: She is proficient at managing large teams.

mis.bad: He is proficient on Excel.
mis.good: He is proficient in Excel.
mis.why: Use "proficient in" or "proficient at", not "on".

def: To officially remove someone from a job, or to refuse to consider an idea.
ex: The company dismissed him after he leaked confidential information to a competitor.
nat: Don't dismiss her suggestion so quickly.

mis.bad: The boss dismissed me from my job.
mis.good: The boss dismissed me.
mis.why: Dismiss already includes the idea of removal, so "from my job" is unnecessary.

def: To end a contract, job, or agreement officially.
ex: The firm terminated the contract after the supplier missed three deadlines in a row.
nat: Your employment will be terminated on the last day of May.

mis.bad: They terminated me by my bad performance.
mis.good: They terminated me because of my poor performance.
mis.why: Use "because of" for the reason, not "by".

def: The ability of a company to keep its employees or customers.
ex: Employee retention improved after the company introduced flexible working hours.
nat: Customer retention is cheaper than finding new clients.

mis.bad: The retention of talents is our priority.
mis.good: The retention of talent is our priority.
mis.why: Talent is uncountable in this sense; do not add -s.

def: The rate at which employees leave and are replaced, or total sales.
ex: High staff turnover is expensive because we keep training new people every month.
nat: The company's annual turnover is about two million pounds.

mis.bad: The turnover of the company is employees leaving.
mis.good: The staff turnover in the company is high.
mis.why: Specify "staff turnover" when talking about people leaving.

def: The total number of people employed.
ex: The board decided to freeze headcount until the end of the financial year.
nat: Our headcount has doubled since last spring.

mis.bad: Our headcount of the company is two hundred.
mis.good: Our company's headcount is two hundred.
mis.why: Headcount stands alone as the number of employees; no extra "of the company" structure.

def: The process of finding and hiring new employees.
ex: Our recruitment process takes about four weeks from the first interview to the offer.
nat: She works in recruitment.

mis.bad: The recruitment of the employes was fast.
mis.good: The recruitment of employees was fast.
mis.why: Correct spelling is employees, and recruitment is uncountable here.

def: To watch and direct a job or group of people.
ex: She oversees a team of fifteen people who handle all our online orders.
nat: Who will oversee the construction work?

mis.bad: He oversees to the project.
mis.good: He oversees the project.
mis.why: Oversee is a transitive verb, with no preposition.

def: A senior person in a company who makes important decisions.
ex: Senior executives met in London to discuss the merger with the competitor.
nat: She became an executive at thirty-five.

mis.bad: The executive of the meeting was Mr. Costa.
mis.good: The executive in charge of the meeting was Mr. Costa.
mis.why: Executive is a senior business person, not the person running a meeting.

def: A person with a lower position than another in an organization.
ex: A good manager listens to subordinates and gives clear feedback.
nat: He treated his subordinates with respect.

mis.bad: My subordinate friends help me a lot.
mis.good: My team members help me a lot.
mis.why: Subordinate is formal and describes rank, not friendship.

def: A system where people are ranked from highest to lowest.
ex: There is a strict hierarchy in the company, and every decision goes through the director.
nat: The hierarchy of the army is very clear.

mis.bad: The company has a hierarchy flat.
mis.good: The company has a flat hierarchy.
mis.why: Adjectives come before the noun in English.

def: A system with many rules and procedures that slow things down.
ex: Too much bureaucracy delayed the project by almost three months.
nat: I hate dealing with government bureaucracy.

mis.bad: The bureaucracy is very slow in this country, many papers.
mis.good: There is a lot of bureaucracy in this country.
mis.why: Bureaucracy is uncountable; use "a lot of".

def: To change how a company is organized to make it work better.
ex: The firm restructured its sales department to reduce costs and improve results.
nat: The company plans to restructure next year.

mis.bad: We restructured our company by cut costs.
mis.good: We restructured our company by cutting costs.
mis.why: After "by", use the -ing form.

def: To make a company smaller by reducing the number of employees.
ex: The company downsized its office and moved most of its staff to remote work.
nat: Many firms downsized during the crisis.

mis.bad: The company downsized to fire fifty people.
mis.good: The company downsized, laying off fifty people.
mis.why: Downsize describes the reduction itself; do not use it with "to + verb" as a purpose in this way.

def: The joining of two companies into one.
ex: The merger created the largest software company in the country.
nat: Employees feared losing their jobs after the merger.

mis.bad: The merge of the two firms was announced.
mis.good: The merger of the two firms was announced.
mis.why: Merge is the verb; the noun is merger.

def: The act of buying a company or getting something.
ex: The acquisition of the small startup cost the company fifty million dollars.
nat: Language acquisition happens naturally in children.

mis.bad: The acquirement of the company was in May.
mis.good: The acquisition of the company was in May.
mis.why: The noun for buying a company is acquisition.

def: The fact of being responsible for your actions and decisions.
ex: Clear accountability helps teams understand who owns each task and each result.
nat: We need more accountability in the process.

mis.bad: The accountability of that error is mine.
mis.good: The responsibility for that error is mine.
mis.why: Accountability is a general principle; for one specific error use "responsibility for".

def: Official permission or authority to do something.
ex: The committee has a clear mandate to review all spending in the department.
nat: The new director has a mandate for change.

mis.bad: The president has a mandate of four years.
mis.good: The president has a four-year term.
mis.why: In English a mandate is authority; the length of office is a term.

def: Supervision of a process, or a mistake caused by not noticing something.
ex: An oversight in the contract allowed the supplier to raise prices without warning.
nat: The committee provides oversight of all spending.

mis.bad: It was an oversight, I did it of purpose.
mis.good: It was an oversight; I did not do it on purpose.
mis.why: An oversight is accidental; "on purpose" is the natural expression.

def: A complete review and improvement of a system or process.
ex: The company needs a complete overhaul of its customer support system.
nat: The engine received a major overhaul.

mis.bad: The overhaul of the system is need.
mis.good: The system needs an overhaul.
mis.why: Need is a verb here: "needs an overhaul".

def: A plan for achieving a long-term goal.
ex: Our marketing strategy changed completely after we studied the new competitors.
nat: They developed a clear strategy for growth.

mis.bad: We need a estrategy for the project.
mis.good: We need a strategy for the project.
mis.why: The English word is strategy.

def: The main purpose of an organization.
ex: Our mission is to make healthcare accessible to everyone in rural areas.
nat: The mission statement is on our website.

mis.bad: The mission of the company is make people happy.
mis.good: The mission of the company is to make people happy.
mis.why: After "is", use "to + verb" to express purpose.

def: To give someone responsibility for something.
ex: The director entrusted her with the most important client in the region.
nat: I would never entrust him with my money.

mis.bad: The manager entrusted to me the project.
mis.good: The manager entrusted me with the project.
mis.why: Use "entrust someone with something" or "entrust something to someone".

def: To tell someone officially that they have done something wrong.
ex: The supervisor reprimanded him for arriving late three times in the same week.
nat: She was reprimanded for ignoring safety rules.

mis.bad: The boss reprimanded to me.
mis.good: The boss reprimanded me.
mis.why: Reprimand is transitive and takes no preposition before the person.

def: The level of confidence and enthusiasm in a group.
ex: Team morale dropped after the company cancelled the annual bonus without any explanation.
nat: A little praise can improve morale.

mis.bad: The moral of the team is very low.
mis.good: The morale of the team is very low.
mis.why: Moral means ethical; the team's mood is morale.

pt: passagem de bastão, transferência de responsabilidades
def: The act of giving responsibility or information to someone else.
ex: Please write a short handover note before you go on holiday.
nat: The handover between shifts takes about fifteen minutes.

mis.bad: I did the handover of my tasks to Ana.
mis.good: I handed over my tasks to Ana.
mis.why: The verb form is "hand over"; the noun is handover.

def: The process of one person taking over a role from another.
ex: The CEO has a clear succession plan for when she retires next year.
nat: A smooth succession is important for family businesses.

mis.bad: We have a plan of succession.
mis.good: We have a succession plan.
mis.why: Succession plan is the usual compound noun.

def: The order of steps in which work is done.
ex: The new software improved our workflow and removed three unnecessary approval steps.
nat: Their workflow is slow and confusing.

mis.bad: I changed my fluxo of work.
mis.good: I changed my workflow.
mis.why: Workflow is one word and means the sequence of work steps.

pt: fazer várias tarefas ao mesmo tempo
def: To do several things at the same time.
ex: I make more mistakes when I am multitasking during a video call.
nat: Some people claim they can multitask easily.

mis.bad: I can multitask well, doing three things on the same time.
mis.good: I can multitask well, doing three things at the same time.
mis.why: The fixed phrase is "at the same time".

def: Doing something well without wasting time or money.
ex: The new system improved the efficiency of our delivery process by thirty percent.
nat: Efficiency matters more than speed.

mis.bad: The efficiency of this machine is more efficient than the old one.
mis.good: This machine is more efficient than the old one.
mis.why: Do not repeat the concept; use the adjective in comparison.

def: To give your attention to one thing.
ex: I turned off my phone so I could focus on the report for two hours.
nat: The meeting focused on next year's budget.

mis.bad: I need to focus in my work.
mis.good: I need to focus on my work.
mis.why: The preposition after focus is "on".

def: Something that stops an activity for a short time.
ex: Constant interruptions from the phone made it hard to finish the report.
nat: We worked for hours without any interruption.

mis.bad: The phone made many interruptions to me.
mis.good: The phone caused me many interruptions.
mis.why: Interruptions are caused, not made.

def: The period of time in which something must happen.
ex: What is the timeframe for completing the migration to the new server?
nat: We need a realistic timeframe.

mis.bad: The project was done in a timeframe of two weeks.
mis.good: The project was done within a timeframe of two weeks.
mis.why: Use "within" a timeframe for a limit.

def: To make something work as well as possible.
ex: We optimized the delivery routes and cut fuel costs by twenty percent.
nat: You can optimize your day by planning ahead.

mis.bad: I optimized my time to better.
mis.good: I optimized my time better.
mis.why: Better is an adverb here; do not add "to".

def: Work that has not been done yet and is waiting.
ex: After the holiday, we had a backlog of more than two hundred support tickets.
nat: The team is trying to clear the backlog.

mis.bad: We have many backlog in the support team.
mis.good: We have a big backlog in the support team.
mis.why: Backlog is countable here; use "a big backlog", not "many".

def: To manage several tasks or responsibilities at once.
ex: She is juggling a full-time job, two projects, and an evening course.
nat: It's hard to juggle work and family.

mis.bad: I juggle between work and studies.
mis.good: I juggle work and studies.
mis.why: Juggle takes a direct object; no "between".

def: Too much work or information at one time.
ex: Information overload makes it difficult to decide which emails are really important.
nat: Many employees feel overloaded in busy seasons.

mis.bad: I have an overload of work.
mis.good: I have too much work.
mis.why: A common simple alternative; "an overload of" is possible but "too much work" is more natural.

def: Working carefully and with steady effort.
ex: She is a diligent employee who always double-checks her numbers before sending a report.
nat: The team was diligent in solving the problem.

mis.bad: He is diligent on his work.
mis.good: He is diligent in his work.
mis.why: Use "diligent in" a task.

def: Very careful about small details.
ex: He is meticulous about documentation and records every change in a shared file.
nat: The report was meticulous and clearly written.

mis.bad: He is meticulous in details.
mis.good: He is meticulous about details.
mis.why: The preposition is "about" with details.

def: Taking action early instead of waiting for problems.
ex: Being proactive means you solve a small problem before it becomes a crisis.
nat: We need a more proactive approach.

mis.bad: He is very proactive of his job.
mis.good: He is very proactive about his job.
mis.why: Use "proactive about" something.

def: Good at finding clever ways to solve problems.
ex: A resourceful assistant found a cheap printer one hour before the presentation.
nat: She is resourceful and rarely needs help.

mis.bad: She is very resourceful in finding solutions.
mis.good: She is very resourceful at finding solutions.
mis.why: Resourceful is followed by "at" plus -ing.

def: The planning and moving of goods, people, or supplies.
ex: Logistics is the hardest part of organizing a conference with five hundred guests.
nat: She manages logistics for a shipping company.

mis.bad: The logistic of the event is complicated.
mis.good: The logistics of the event are complicated.
mis.why: Logistics always ends in -s, and takes the plural verb in this use.

def: The goods a business has in stock.
ex: We count the inventory every Friday to make sure nothing has been lost.
nat: The shop has a large inventory.

mis.bad: Our stock list is the inventory.
mis.good: We keep a record of our inventory.
mis.why: Inventory means goods in stock or the list of them.

def: A company that provides goods or services to another.
ex: Our main supplier delayed the shipment by a week because of a strike.
nat: We are looking for a cheaper supplier.

mis.bad: We bought from a fornecer in China.
mis.good: We bought from a supplier in China.
mis.why: The English noun is supplier.

def: The process of buying goods or services for a company.
ex: The procurement team compares at least three offers before buying new equipment.
nat: Public procurement must follow strict rules.

mis.bad: The procurement of the group is the buyer.
mis.good: The procurement team is responsible for buying.
mis.why: Procurement is a process or department, not a person.

def: A quantity of goods sent together.
ex: The shipment arrived two days late, and the customer demanded a discount.
nat: We are waiting for a large shipment of parts.

mis.bad: The shipment of the goods was in ship.
mis.good: The shipment of goods went by sea.
mis.why: Use "by sea" for transport method.

def: A large building where goods are stored.
ex: The company keeps most of its products in a warehouse near the port.
nat: He works in a warehouse.

mis.bad: I work in the deposit of the company.
mis.good: I work in the warehouse of the company.
mis.why: The Portuguese "depósito" for a storage building is "warehouse".

def: To make goods in large numbers with machines.
ex: The shoes are manufactured in Vietnam and sold in more than forty countries.
nat: The company manufactures car parts.

mis.bad: The product is manufactured by China.
mis.good: The product is manufactured in China.
mis.why: Place of manufacture uses "in", not "by".

def: Regular business costs such as rent and electricity.
ex: Rent and electricity are the biggest overhead for our small office.
nat: We reduced overhead by moving to a smaller building.

mis.bad: The overheads is expensive here.
mis.good: The overhead is expensive here.
mis.why: Both forms exist, but subject and verb must agree: "overheads are" or "overhead is".

def: Money earned after paying all costs.
ex: The company made a profit of two million dollars in its first year.
nat: We hope to turn a profit by December.

mis.bad: The profit from the lucrative company is big.
mis.good: The company made a big profit.
mis.why: Make a profit is the natural collocation.

def: The difference between cost and selling price.
ex: Our profit margin is very small because raw materials have become more expensive.
nat: The firm works on a thin margin.

mis.bad: The margin of lucro is ten percent.
mis.good: The profit margin is ten percent.
mis.why: Use "profit margin" as the compound.

def: A company owned or controlled by a larger company.
ex: The bank opened a subsidiary in Argentina to serve local clients.
nat: It is a wholly owned subsidiary of a Japanese group.

mis.bad: The subsidiary of my company is in Chile.
mis.good: My company has a subsidiary in Chile.
mis.why: Subsidiary is a company owned by another, so the phrasing should show who owns it.

def: A business that sells the right to use its name and products.
ex: He bought a coffee franchise and opened three shops within five years.
nat: The franchise gives owners strong support.

mis.bad: He opened a franchising of pizza.
mis.good: He opened a pizza franchise.
mis.why: The noun for the business is franchise.

def: A new company, especially one that uses technology.
ex: She left her bank job to join a small tech startup in Recife.
nat: The startup received funding from investors.

mis.bad: My startup is a company that has many years.
mis.good: My startup is a young company.
mis.why: A startup is by definition new.

def: A person who starts and runs a business and takes risks.
ex: The young entrepreneur started her online shop in her parents' garage.
nat: Many entrepreneurs fail before they succeed.

mis.bad: He is an entrepeneur of success.
mis.good: He is a successful entrepreneur.
mis.why: The adjective goes before the noun; also check the spelling.

def: A new business project that involves risk.
ex: Their first venture failed, but they learned a lot and tried again.
nat: It's a joint venture between two firms.

mis.bad: They have a joint venture with the two companies of Brazil.
mis.good: They have a joint venture with two Brazilian companies.
mis.why: Use adjectives like Brazilian before the noun and avoid awkward "of".

def: A company or person trying to win in the same market.
ex: Our competitors lowered their prices, so we had to change our strategy.
nat: He is our biggest competitor.

mis.bad: We have a concurrent in the same city.
mis.good: We have a competitor in the same city.
mis.why: "Concorrente" is a competitor in English.

def: All the customers of a business.
ex: The restaurant has a wealthy clientele who often book tables months in advance.
nat: The shop is trying to attract a younger clientele.

mis.bad: The clientele are very happy with the service.
mis.good: The clientele is very happy with the service.
mis.why: Clientele is normally singular in this use.

def: The selling of goods in large amounts, usually to shops.
ex: We buy fabric at wholesale and sell clothes in our own shop.
nat: The wholesale price is much lower.

mis.bad: I buy in the wholesale for my shop.
mis.good: I buy wholesale for my shop.
mis.why: Use "buy wholesale" without the article.

def: Goods that are bought and sold.
ex: The store keeps its best merchandise near the entrance to attract more customers.
nat: All merchandise is half price this weekend.

mis.bad: The merchandises were damaged.
mis.good: The merchandise was damaged.
mis.why: Merchandise is uncountable and has no plural -s.

def: The main office of a company.
ex: The company's headquarters is in Dublin, but it has offices worldwide.
nat: They moved their headquarters to Berlin.

mis.bad: The headquarter of the firm is in Rome.
mis.good: The headquarters of the firm is in Rome.
mis.why: Headquarters has an -s even when it refers to one place.

def: One of several local offices of a larger organization.
ex: I went to the bank branch near my house to open a savings account.
nat: The company has a branch in every major city.

mis.bad: I work in the filial of Curitiba.
mis.good: I work in the Curitiba branch.
mis.why: The business word for filial is branch.

def: An estimate of future numbers based on current information.
ex: The sales projections for next year are based on the current growth rate.
nat: Their projections were too optimistic.

mis.bad: The projection of the vendas is high.
mis.good: The sales projection is high.
mis.why: Use "sales projection" in English.

def: A small test of a new idea before it is used widely.
ex: We ran a pilot in two stores before introducing the system nationwide.
nat: The pilot program lasted three months.

mis.bad: We did a pilot test of the idea before.
mis.good: We ran a pilot before launching the idea.
mis.why: Run a pilot is a common collocation.

def: The gradual introduction of a new product or system.
ex: The rollout of the new software will begin in the sales department next week.
nat: There were problems during the rollout.

mis.bad: The rollout of the system was in steps.
mis.good: The system was rolled out in phases.
mis.why: "Roll out" is the verb form, used naturally in the passive.

def: To start using a plan, system, or decision.
ex: The bank implemented the new security rules in all its branches last month.
nat: We need to implement these changes quickly.

mis.bad: We implemented the system in the company since January.
mis.good: We have used the system in the company since January.
mis.why: Since requires a present perfect form with a continuing action.

def: The ability of something to succeed or be financially sound.
ex: The study will test the commercial viability of the new product.
nat: Investors questioned the viability of the plan.

mis.bad: The viability of project is high.
mis.good: The viability of the project is high.
mis.why: Do not forget the article before project.

def: The act of working together to achieve something.
ex: The product was developed in close collaboration with several of our customers.
nat: Collaboration between the two teams improved results.

mis.bad: The collaboration of the two teams was a success of work.
mis.good: The collaboration between the two teams was a success.
mis.why: Collaboration between two groups uses "between".

def: Extra benefit from two groups or ideas working together.
ex: The merger created synergy between the design and engineering departments.
nat: There is real synergy in this team.

mis.bad: The synergy among the two teams is great.
mis.good: The synergy between the two teams is great.
mis.why: Use "between" with two groups.

def: Friendship and trust among people who spend time together.
ex: There is great camaraderie among the nurses because they work long shifts together.
nat: The camaraderie of the team helped us finish.

mis.bad: The camaradery of the group is big.
mis.good: There is great camaraderie in the group.
mis.why: Spelling camaraderie; also use "great", not "big".

def: A person who is in the same team as you.
ex: My teammates helped me finish the presentation when I got sick.
nat: He is a great teammate.

mis.bad: I have a good relation with my teamates.
mis.good: I have a good relationship with my teammates.
mis.why: Relation is not the same as relationship, and spelling teammates.

def: A person of the same age or level as you.
ex: She was respected by her peers because she always shared her knowledge.
nat: Feedback from peers is very useful.

mis.bad: My peers of work are older than me.
mis.good: My colleagues at work are older than me.
mis.why: Peer is formal; for work friends use colleagues.

def: Working well together as one united group.
ex: The coach built a cohesive team that played well even under pressure.
nat: A cohesive plan is easier to follow.

mis.bad: The group is cohesive between them.
mis.good: The group is cohesive.
mis.why: Cohesive already refers to the group; "between them" is not needed.

def: To bring people together to support something.
ex: The manager rallied the team after the failed launch and set new goals.
nat: Employees rallied around their new boss.

mis.bad: The team rallied to around the new leader.
mis.good: The team rallied around the new leader.
mis.why: Use "rally around" without "to".

def: A serious disagreement between people or groups.
ex: A conflict between two managers slowed down every decision in the department.
nat: They tried to avoid conflict.

mis.bad: They had a conflict with each other of ideas.
mis.good: They had a conflict of ideas.
mis.why: Do not add "with each other" after conflict of ideas.

def: Helpful and intended to improve something.
ex: She gave me constructive feedback that helped me improve my presentation skills.
nat: We had a constructive discussion.

mis.bad: He gave me a constructive critic.
mis.good: He gave me constructive criticism.
mis.why: The noun is criticism; critic is a person.

def: The feeling of being responsible for your work, or legal right of owning.
ex: Good employees take ownership of their mistakes and fix them quickly.
nat: Who has ownership of this data?

mis.bad: He took the ownership for the problem.
mis.good: He took ownership of the problem.
mis.why: Take ownership of, without an article.

def: Support between people who share the same aims.
ex: Workers showed solidarity by refusing to work extra hours without pay.
nat: They expressed solidarity with the victims.

mis.bad: They did solidarity with the strikers.
mis.good: They showed solidarity with the strikers.
mis.why: Show solidarity is the natural collocation.

def: A question asking for information.
ex: We receive about fifty customer inquiries a day by email and phone.
nat: I made an inquiry about prices.

mis.bad: I did an inquiry about the price.
mis.good: I made an inquiry about the price.
mis.why: Make an inquiry is the natural verb choice.

def: The feeling of being pleased because your needs are met.
ex: Customer satisfaction rose after we reduced the waiting time on the phone.
nat: She felt great satisfaction after finishing the project.

mis.bad: I am satisfaction with the service.
mis.good: I am satisfied with the service.
mis.why: Satisfied is the adjective after "am"; satisfaction is a noun.

def: Money given to make up for a loss or a problem.
ex: The airline offered passengers compensation for the six-hour delay of the flight.
nat: He asked for compensation for the damage.

mis.bad: I asked for a compensation of the delay.
mis.good: I asked for compensation for the delay.
mis.why: Compensation is uncountable here and takes "for".

def: Polite and showing respect.
ex: The receptionist was courteous even when the visitor was rude to her.
nat: Please be courteous to all customers.

mis.bad: The staff were courteous with the clients.
mis.good: The staff were courteous to the clients.
mis.why: Use "courteous to" a person.

def: Listening and paying careful attention to someone's needs.
ex: The waiters were very attentive and refilled our glasses before we asked.
nat: She is an attentive listener.

mis.bad: The staff was attentive of my needs.
mis.good: The staff was attentive to my needs.
mis.why: Use "attentive to".

def: A telephone service that gives advice or help.
ex: I called the helpline, but I had to wait twenty minutes to talk to someone.
nat: The helpline is open all night.

mis.bad: I called to the helpline.
mis.good: I called the helpline.
mis.why: Call is transitive, so no "to" is needed.

def: To find a solution to a problem or disagreement.
ex: The support team resolved the issue within an hour and apologized to the customer.
nat: We hope to resolve this quickly.

mis.bad: The problem was resolved to me by the staff.
mis.good: The staff resolved the problem for me.
mis.why: Use the active form with "for me".

def: The solution to a problem or the end of a disagreement.
ex: The company promised a quick resolution to the billing problem.
nat: The two sides reached a peaceful resolution.

mis.bad: I wait for the resolution of my problem since Monday.
mis.good: I have been waiting for a resolution to my problem since Monday.
mis.why: Since needs the present perfect continuous.

def: A written statement by a customer praising a product or service.
ex: The website includes testimonials from clients who have used our service for years.
nat: Positive testimonials build trust.

mis.bad: The testemunial of the client was good.
mis.good: The client's testimonial was good.
mis.why: Check the spelling and possessive form.

def: The general opinion that people have about someone or something.
ex: The restaurant has a good reputation for fast service and fresh food.
nat: His reputation was damaged by the scandal.

mis.bad: The company has a bad reputation of customer service.
mis.good: The company has a bad reputation for customer service.
mis.why: Use "reputation for".

def: Friendly feelings and trust between a company and its customers.
ex: A free replacement is a small price to pay for customer goodwill.
nat: The company lost a lot of goodwill after the scandal.

mis.bad: It was a gesture of good will to the client.
mis.good: It was a gesture of goodwill to the client.
mis.why: Goodwill is written as one word.

def: Help given to someone.
ex: Thank you for your assistance; the technician solved my problem in minutes.
nat: Do you need any assistance?

mis.bad: I need an assistance with my account.
mis.good: I need assistance with my account.
mis.why: Assistance is uncountable, so no article.

def: Quick to reply and react to what people need.
ex: The support team is very responsive and usually answers emails within fifteen minutes.
nat: We want to be responsive to client needs.

mis.bad: The team is responsive of our needs.
mis.good: The team is responsive to our needs.
mis.why: Use "responsive to".

def: Not answering or reacting when asked.
ex: The supplier was unresponsive for a week, so we looked for another company.
nat: The website is unresponsive today.

mis.bad: He is unresponsive for my emails.
mis.good: He is unresponsive to my emails.
mis.why: Use "unresponsive to".

def: A formal complaint about unfair treatment.
ex: She filed a grievance with HR after her manager refused to approve her leave.
nat: The union listened to the workers' grievances.

mis.bad: She made a grievance against the company.
mis.good: She filed a grievance against the company.
mis.why: File a grievance is the standard collocation.

def: To correct something that is wrong.
ex: The bank rectified the error on my account and refunded the extra fee.
nat: We'll rectify the situation immediately.

mis.bad: We will rectify the problem for correct it.
mis.good: We will rectify the problem to correct it.
mis.why: Use "to + verb" for purpose, not "for".

def: To pay back money someone spent.
ex: The company reimbursed me for my train ticket after the business trip.
nat: Will they reimburse the cost of the hotel?

mis.bad: The company reimbursed to me the ticket.
mis.good: The company reimbursed me for the ticket.
mis.why: Reimburse takes the person directly, then "for".

def: Not happy with something you received.
ex: Dissatisfied customers can damage a small business by writing bad online reviews.
nat: He was dissatisfied with the repair.

mis.bad: I am dissatisfied of the service.
mis.good: I am dissatisfied with the service.
mis.why: Use "dissatisfied with".

def: To provide for someone's needs or fit them in.
ex: We will try to accommodate your request for a later delivery date.
nat: The hotel can accommodate two hundred guests.

mis.bad: The hotel accommodates to two hundred people.
mis.good: The hotel accommodates two hundred people.
mis.why: Accommodate is transitive and has no "to".

def: A small problem that causes trouble or annoyance.
ex: We apologize for any inconvenience caused by the delay in your delivery.
nat: The closure caused great inconvenience to travelers.

mis.bad: Sorry for the inconvenients.
mis.good: Sorry for the inconvenience.
mis.why: Inconvenience is the correct noun.

def: Showing that you are sorry about something.
ex: The manager was very apologetic about the mistake and offered a full refund.
nat: She gave an apologetic smile.

mis.bad: He was apologetic of the delay.
mis.good: He was apologetic about the delay.
mis.why: Use "apologetic about".

def: A person or company that pays for professional services.
ex: I have a call with an important client from Germany at three o'clock.
nat: She works with corporate clients.

mis.bad: The doctor has many costumers.
mis.good: The lawyer has many clients.
mis.why: Professionals have clients; shops have customers. Also "costumer" is not "customer".

def: Money paid to an employee every month for their job.
ex: My salary goes up by five percent every year if my manager approves it.
nat: What salary are you expecting for this job?

mis.bad: I receive a salary of the month.
mis.good: I receive a fixed salary every month.
mis.why: "Salary of the month" is a literal translation; say a monthly or fixed salary.

def: A person who is paid to work for a company.
ex: The company has about three hundred employees working in four different countries.
nat: Every new employee gets a laptop on the first day.

mis.bad: I am an employe of this company.
mis.good: I am an employee of this company.
mis.why: The word ends in -ee, with a double e.

def: A person or company that pays people to work for them.
ex: My employer allows us to work from home on Mondays and Fridays.
nat: The bank is the largest employer in the town.

mis.bad: My employer are very kind.
mis.good: My employer is very kind.
mis.why: Employer is singular here, so the verb is "is".

def: A section of a company that has a specific job.
ex: She moved to the marketing department after working in sales for three years.
nat: Which department do you work in?

mis.bad: I work at the department of marketing in a company.
mis.good: I work in the marketing department of a company.
mis.why: The natural order is "marketing department" with the preposition "in".

def: The place where people work.
ex: A friendly workplace makes people happier and more productive during the week.
nat: Safety in the workplace is very important.

mis.bad: I like the ambient of my workplace.
mis.good: I like the atmosphere of my workplace.
mis.why: "Ambient" is not the common noun here; use atmosphere.

def: The series of jobs a person has during their working life.
ex: He started his career as a waiter and now owns three restaurants.
nat: She wants to change her career.

mis.bad: I want to make a career in this company.
mis.good: I want to build a career in this company.
mis.why: The usual verb is "build" a career, not "make".

def: A short course where people learn practical skills.
ex: I attended a workshop on public speaking, and it really boosted my confidence.
nat: The workshop starts at nine tomorrow.

mis.bad: I did a workshop about presentations in the last week.
mis.good: I attended a workshop about presentations last week.
mis.why: Attend is the natural verb, and there is no "in the last week".

def: A talk that gives information to a group of people.
ex: My presentation lasted twenty minutes, and the clients asked many questions at the end.
nat: She gave a great presentation yesterday.

mis.bad: I made a presentation to the audience yesterday.
mis.good: I gave a presentation to the audience yesterday.
mis.why: The usual verb is "give" a presentation.

def: An arrangement to meet someone at a particular time.
ex: I have an appointment with the accountant at ten tomorrow morning.
nat: You need an appointment to see the director.

mis.bad: I have a compromise with my doctor tomorrow.
mis.good: I have an appointment with my doctor tomorrow.
mis.why: "Compromise" is a false friend; a scheduled meeting is an appointment.

def: A large meeting where people discuss a subject.
ex: The company paid for me to attend a technology conference in Madrid.
nat: The conference lasts three days.

mis.bad: I went to a conference of marketing.
mis.good: I went to a marketing conference.
mis.why: The topic noun comes before conference: a marketing conference.

def: A piece of work that must be done.
ex: Our first task is to find out why the customers are leaving.
nat: It is a difficult task.

mis.bad: I did my tasks in the day.
mis.good: I finished my tasks during the day.
mis.why: Use "during the day"; "in the day" is not natural here.

def: The act of working well together as a group.
ex: Good teamwork helped us finish the project two weeks before the deadline.
nat: Teamwork is important in my job.

mis.bad: The teamwork of the group are great.
mis.good: The teamwork in the group is great.
mis.why: Teamwork is singular and uncountable.

def: The ability to guide and motivate other people.
ex: Her leadership during the crisis kept the whole team calm and focused.
nat: Strong leadership is needed now.

mis.bad: He has lead skills in the company.
mis.good: He has leadership skills in the company.
mis.why: The noun is leadership; "lead" is a verb.

def: How well someone or something does a job.
ex: Her performance in the first quarter was much better than anyone expected.
nat: The performance of the new server is excellent.

mis.bad: My performance of the work was bad.
mis.good: My performance at work was bad.
mis.why: Use "at work" for performance in a job context.

def: A person who buys goods or services from a business.
ex: Our customers prefer to pay online instead of coming to the shop.
nat: The customer is always right.

mis.bad: He is my customer friend.
mis.good: He is a regular customer of mine.
mis.why: English puts the adjective before the noun and uses "of mine".

def: A person who watches and directs the work of others.
ex: My supervisor reviews my reports every Friday and gives me advice.
nat: Please talk to your supervisor first.

mis.bad: My supervisor said to me to wait.
mis.good: My supervisor told me to wait.
mis.why: After "tell" use a direct person; "said to me to" is wrong.

def: A person who is in charge of a team or a department.
ex: The manager called a meeting to explain the changes in the sales policy.
nat: She is the manager of a small hotel.

mis.bad: My manager is the person that I have to obey, he is my chief.
mis.good: My manager is my boss.
mis.why: Boss is the common word for the person you report to.

def: All the people who work in a company.
ex: The staff were invited to a party at the end of the year.
nat: We need more staff in the kitchen.

mis.bad: The staffs of the company are happy.
mis.good: The staff of the company are happy.
mis.why: Staff is a collective noun and has no plural -s.

def: Lasting for a long time or for ever.
ex: After one year, they offered me a permanent contract with better benefits.
nat: He is looking for a permanent job.

mis.bad: I got a permanent job of five years.
mis.good: I got a permanent job after five years.
mis.why: Permanent means no end date; "of five years" suggests a fixed period.

def: Lasting only for a short time.
ex: She took a temporary job in a bakery during the summer holidays.
nat: This is only a temporary solution.

mis.bad: I work here temporary.
mis.good: I work here temporarily.
mis.why: The adverb is temporarily; temporary is an adjective.

def: Having the education or experience needed for a job.
ex: He is a fully qualified electrician with fifteen years of experience in industrial buildings.
nat: We need a qualified engineer.

mis.bad: He is qualified to this job.
mis.good: He is qualified for this job.
mis.why: Use "qualified for" a job.

def: To give someone a job and pay them.
ex: The company hired fifty new workers before the busy Christmas season began.
nat: We are planning to hire a designer.

mis.bad: They hired me to work in the sales.
mis.good: They hired me to work in sales.
mis.why: There is no article before a department name like "sales".

def: Documents and forms that you must complete.
ex: I spent the whole morning filling out paperwork for my new visa.
nat: There is too much paperwork in this job.

mis.bad: I have many paperworks to finish.
mis.good: I have a lot of paperwork to finish.
mis.why: Paperwork is uncountable and has no plural.

def: A person who does office work or serves customers in a shop.
ex: The hotel clerk gave me a key and explained where the breakfast room was.
nat: He works as a bank clerk.

mis.bad: He is a clerc in a store.
mis.good: He is a clerk in a store.
mis.why: The spelling is clerk, with a k.

def: A person whose job is to welcome visitors and answer calls.
ex: The receptionist asked me to sign in and wait in the lobby.
nat: She works as a receptionist at a dental clinic.

mis.bad: I talked with the reception of the hotel.
mis.good: I talked to the receptionist at the hotel.
